articles.title: New Trailer for OWN Documentary on All-Black Women's Volleyball Team Drops Ahead of Premiere Date
articles.summary: "We Belong Here: The Story of Team Dream," a documentary chronicling the first-ever all-Black women's professional volleyball team, will debut on the Oprah Winfrey Network on Saturday, September 26 at 9 p.m. ET.
articles.body:
"We Belong Here: The Story of Team Dream," a documentary chronicling the first-ever all-Black women's professional volleyball team, will debut on the Oprah Winfrey Network on Saturday, September 26 at 9 p.m. ET.

"Told entirely through the voices of the women themselves, with no external narrator, 'We Belong Here: The Story of Team Dream,' is a story of triumph. The film honors the athletes' resilience, joy, humor, friendship, and pride, while acknowledging the systemic barriers they faced. At its heart, it is a story about determination, community, and the power of belonging."

As noted in the release, the team was led by former Texas volleyball superstar, two-time AVCA First Team All American and NCAA national champion Haley Eckerman.

The team had "limited practice," per the release. However, that didn't stop Team Dream from a dominant performance. Team Dream went 7-0 overall, winning gold in the five-team tournament .

It wasn't easy all along the way. Team Dream had a pair of tough five-set matches in the playoff bracket, especially in the semifinals, when the squad was down two sets to zero against Team Freedom. However, Team Dream rallied for the 3-2 win before doing the same against Hoosier Exterminators for the triumphant victory.

The documentary, which was produced by Bunim/Murray Productions (a Banijay Americas company), has already premiered at the Martha's Vineyard African American Film Festival.

articles.title: Barry Melrose, hockey player and coach-turned-broadcaster, dies at 70
articles.summary: Melrose stepped away from his analyst role in 2023 after he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
articles.body: Barry Melrose, a hockey player-turned-coach who led the Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup Final before going on to a long career in broadcasting the sport, has died. He was 70. ESPN announced Melrose’s death Wednesday after his wife informed the network. “From the flowing locks of his distinctive mullet to the flared lapels of his trademark long suit coats, Barry Melrose cut an unmistakable figure whenever you were fortunate enough to run into him at a rink or catch him on your television screen,” NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said. “You were even more fortunate if you engaged him in conversation or listened to his analysis because he never failed to boost your love of the game of hockey.” Melrose stepped away from his analyst role in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. Wayne Gretzky at the time said Melrose was “bigger than any team.” Melrose had a relatable everyman’s broadcasting style, bringing a sense of humor to his insights, and was easily recognized by his goatee and slicked-back hair. “For decades, Barry Melrose was one of the most distinctive and trusted voices in hockey,” ESPN said in a statement. “His knowledge of the game was deep, his candor was refreshing and his passion was unmistakable.” From rural Kelvington, Saskatchewan, Melrose broke into pro hockey with the Cincinnati Stingers of the now-defunct World Hockey Association in 1976. He played three seasons in Cincinnati — the last teaming with a young Mark Messier — and, following the WHA’s demise, made the transition to the NHL with Winnipeg in 1979. Melrose went on to play for Toronto and Detroit, where he closed his career following the 1985-86 season. He finished with 10 goals and 33 points and 728 penalty minutes in 300 career NHL regular-season games, and he skated in seven more in the playoffs. His WHA totals were five goals and 32 points and 343 penalty minutes in 178 games with Cincinnati. Melrose turned to coaching and led the Adirondack Red Wings to win the American Hockey League Calder Cup championship in 1992. The following year, Melrose was hired by the Kings, where he brought a sense of colorful flair and instant success to Los Angeles. In his rookie season, he coached a Kings team that featured Gretzky to make a memorable playoff run. They reached the final before losing to Montreal in five games. Melrose finished with a record of 79-101 and 29 ties over two-plus seasons in L.A. before being fired midway through the 1994-95 season. He was hired by ESPN in 1996 and left broadcasting for what became a brief stint coaching the Tampa Bay Lightning in Steven Stamkos’ rookie season in 2008-09. Melrose was fired 16 games into the season following a 5-7-4 start and returned to broadcasting. Melrose also was known for his long-ball hitting prowess in fast-pitch softball, joining fellow Kelvington-area NHL players Wendel Clark, Joey Kocur, Kelly Chase and Kevin Kaminski and others in the offseason in Saskatchewan to form what some call “the toughest team there ever was.”

images.caption: FILE - Former Los Angeles Kings coach Barry Melrose speaks to fans as he is honored prior to an NHL hockey game between the Kings and the Calgary Flames, on Feb. 12, 2015, in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Avinash Sable eyes Asian Games double, 5,000m qualification in Indian Athletics Series final
articles.summary: More sports News: New Delhi: With an Asian Games double in his sights, Avinash Sable will put his steeplechase skills to the test at the Indian Athletics Series final h.
articles.body: New Delhi: With an Asian Games double in his sights, Avinash Sable will put his steeplechase skills to the test at the Indian Athletics Series final here on Thursday while also chasing the 5,000m qualification mark of 13:39.18 seconds.The Athletics Federation of India (AFI) is seeking approval from the Aichi-Nagoya Games organisers for Sable to contest the 5,000m alongside his confirmed 3,000m steeplechase event. But the Hangzhou Asian Games gold medallist must first breach the AFI qualification mark at the JLN stadium.“I am looking forward to evaluating my skills in Thursday’s race before the Japan Asian Games,” Sable said on Wednesday. “Negotiating water jumps in the steeplechase race is an important part of the strategy,” he added.It has been nearly 14 months since the national record holder last competed in the gruelling event featuring seven water barriers and 28 fixed hurdles. Sable suffered an injury at the 2025 Monaco Diamond League and has since undergone rehabilitation.“I’m mentally and physically strong enough to face any challenge during the Games,” he said. Sable won steeplechase gold and 5,000m silver at the Hangzhou Games in 2023 and hopes to win two medals in Japan. His national record is 8:09.91, set at the 2024 Paris Diamond League.Attention will also be on the quartermilers and the women’s 4x400m team.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: IOA forms committee to probe Asunta Lakra’s harassment charge
articles.summary: Hockey News: Kolkata: Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president PT Usha’s decision to constitute an independent inquiry committee to examine former India women’s .
articles.body: Kolkata: Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president PT Usha’s decision to constitute an independent inquiry committee to examine former India women’s hockey captain Asunta Lakra’s complaint has been welcomed by Hockey India (HI) executive board member and vice-president Asima Ali, who called for “strict and immediate action” against those found responsible.Lakra had alleged in her email to Union sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya, the Sports Authority of India (SAI) and TOPS officials in July that, after informing the Jharkhand govt about allegations of sexual harassment against former Eklavya Hockey Centre coach Sudhir Golla, she was threatened by HI secretary general and Hockey Jharkhand president Bhola Nath Singh for speaking up.“It’s a great step. I’m very happy with what Ma’am PT Usha has done. It should have been done earlier, but at least they have done it now. Strict and immediate action should be taken against the culprits,” Ali said.In a letter dated Sept 7, IOA informed HI that it had constituted the committee following the federation’s request to the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports on July 15 and the ministry’s subsequent request to IOA on July 16.The committee will be chaired by retired Justice Deepa Sharma, with Vandana Rao, Mamta Kharb and Sitwat Nabi as members. IOA said the committee would function independently and impartially. HI has been asked to bear the committee’s honorarium and expenses, including travel, accommodation and incidental expenses.IOA president Usha’s letter to HI also stated, “Hockey India is also requested to extend its full cooperation to the Committee and to ensure that all relevant records, documents, information and such other assistance as may be required are made available to the Committee in a timely manner, so as to enable it to discharge its mandate effectively and expeditiously.”Ali said she would extend her full support to the committee and cooperate with its proceedings. “The committee has my complete support. Asunta is also there. I don’t know about the rest,” she said.The HI vice-president also criticised attempts to silence people within the sport before adding, “Bhola Nath should be investigated for allegedly using Hockey India funds for the case that I have filed against him in the Delhi High Court, and the amount should be recovered immediately by Hockey India.”Singh has already denied the allegations made by Lakra, calling them baseless. Golla has also rejected the allegations and demanded a fair inquiry.The dispute between HI and Lakra took a further turn when HI’s Ethics Committee, headed by retired Justice Raghvendra Kumar, initiated a fact-finding inquiry into complaints filed against Lakra by Jharkhand player Albela Rani Toppo. Lakra termed the move “intimidation” and urged the sports minister to intervene and stop the Ethics Committee inquiry against her.With IOA now setting up an independent committee to examine Lakra’s allegations, the focus will be on whether the inquiry brings clarity to the competing complaints and establishes accountability.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Noah Lyles eyes 2028 Olympic title defence after injury ends season
articles.summary: More sports News: Noah Lyles wasn’t planning on playing ‘commentator’ ahead of the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship.The reigning men’s Olympic 100m champ.
articles.body: Noah Lyles wasn’t planning on playing ‘commentator’ ahead of the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship.The reigning men’s Olympic 100m champion had been looking forward to joining the sport’s biggest stars at World Athletics’ new season-ending showpiece in Budapest, until injury forced him to end his season early.In a video call with reporters on Tuesday, Lyles grinned when he was asked a couple of times for his views on some of his rivals who will be in action this weekend. “Shoot, I usually focus more on myself than other people,” Lyles said in response to a question about his American compatriot Kenny Bednarek attempting the sprint double in Budapest. When the very next question was about what impression he had of some of the South African sprinters, the 29-year-old smiled again while going on to say, “I’m not here to be a commentator of sorts today. That’s not really my goal.”And then came a question about 2027. The conversation was about Noah Lyles once again. And the four-time 200m world champion was only too happy to look ahead to what he considers the ‘building blocks’ in his quest to defend his Olympic 100m crown on home soil in Los Angeles.“I am very excited for 2027. It’s going to be a lot of fun,” Lyles said. “2027 is the building block for 2028. And let’s get that plan smooth and polished so that when we go into 2028, we’re just following the blueprint because we know it’s going to work.”Though he sustained his season-ending injury at the US nationals in July, Lyles managed to run two 9.7-second races at the event before the setback, leaving even himself a little ‘shocked’.“I don’t like to put limits on myself,” Lyles said. “In my head, American records definitely come in touching the stars, going after anything and everything. I think I kind of shocked myself a little bit by running those two 9.7s at the nationals because although I was prepared to run fast, I wasn’t prepared to do it then.“So it’s proven to myself that I can run very fast, even though I’m not 100% perfect with my first 30 (metres), which was a super exciting thing. So there’s a lot more to come for 2027 and 2028.”The competitive absence of Lyles is undoubtedly a blow to an event World Athletics has billed as ‘the best of the best’ with a record $10m prize purse on offer. But there’s still a lot on the programme to keep athletics fans hooked, the 1500m race in particular one of the event’s top attractions, seeing as it is set to reignite the rivalry between Great Britain’s Josh Kerr and Norway’s Jakob Ingebrigtsen.Ingebrigtsen’s recent criticism of Kerr for skipping the European Championships last month may well have added a layer of spice to their upcoming showdown. “Always under criticism,” Kerr, who clocked 3:42.66 in the mile at the London Diamond League in July to break Hicham El Guerrouj’s 27-year-old world record, said with a wry chuckle in response to his fierce rival’s comments.“Every person is different, and every athlete is different in the way that they approach the season. For me, the way that I approach it is circling two to four big dates and working my way around those and also to get in and out of a year without massive problems,” added the Scot, who won the 1500m gold at the 2023 world championships in Budapest.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: India demolish Pakistan 19-0 to storm into Women’s Hockey Junior Asia Cup semi-finals
articles.summary: Hockey News: India booked their place in the semi-finals of the 2026 Women’s Junior Asia Cup after beating Pakistan 19-0 in the quarter-final in Moqi, China, on Th.
articles.body: India booked their place in the semi-finals of the 2026 Women’s Junior Asia Cup after beating Pakistan 19-0 in the quarter-final in Moqi, China, on Thursday.The defending champions had already topped their group after beating Japan, Malaysia and South Korea. They will now face the winner of the South Korea vs Malaysia quarter-final for a place in the final.India took the lead in the seventh minute through Puja Sahoo and continued to score throughout the match. Roshni Aind doubled the lead two minutes later before Tanushree Dinesh Kadu, Sukhveer Kaur and Sanika Chandrakant Mane added more goals.Mane scored again in the 23rd minute, while Tanuja Toppo, Pooja Malik and Purnima Yadav also found the net before half-time. India went into the break 10-0 ahead.The goals continued after the restart. Malik completed her hat-trick with goals in the 49th and 51st minutes, while Supriya scored twice. Krishna Sharma, Binima Dhan and Roshni also added to Pakistan's problems, with Roshni scoring again in the final minute to complete the 19-0 win.India are now two wins away from completing a hat-trick of Women’s Junior Asia Cup titles. They won the tournament in 2023 and 2024.India’s goals:Puja Sahoo – 7'Roshni Aind – 9', 60+'Tanushree Dinesh Kadu – 11'Sukhveer Kaur – 13'Sanika Chandrakant Mane – 13', 23'Madhu Sidar – 16', 39'Geeta Yadav – 18'Tanuja Toppo – 25'Pooja Malik – 27', 49', 51'Purnima Yadav – 33'Supriya – 40', 54'Krishna Sharma – 48'Binima Dhan – 55' Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Maica García denunciará ante la justicia al Sabadell tras no renovarla después de ser madre
articles.standfirst: La nueva jugadora del CN Sant Andreu rompe su silencio y se muestra muy dolida con el club de su vida
articles.summary: La nueva jugadora del CN Sant Andreu rompe su silencio y se muestra muy dolida con el club de su vida
articles.body: La campeona olímpica y mundial Maica García denunciará ante la justicia al Astralpool Sabadell después de que el club le comunicara que no contaba con ella para la próxima temporada tras regresar de su permiso de maternidad. La nueva jugadora del CN Sant Andreu rompió este jueves su silencio tras la decisión del club vallesano y aseguró que no se merece este desenlace después de 32 años de relación con una entidad que considera "su vida". "El Sabadell es mi vida y será mi club toda mi vida. Soy de aquí, he crecido aquí. Las personas van y vienen, las personas del club van y vienen. Me voy muy dolida por unas personas que llevan este club. Estoy descontenta con esta gestión, no me lo merezco, yo ni nadie", apuntó la boya española. García explicó su situación en las instalaciones de su nuevo equipo, el CN Sant Andreu, donde repasó los meses transcurridos desde que comunicó su embarazo, en enero de 2025, hasta su salida del club vallesano. Tras dar a luz, inició su regreso a los entrenamientos con la convicción de que su vínculo contractual con el Sabadell se extendía hasta el 31 de agosto de 2027. Su interpretación se apoyaba en el artículo 6 bis del Real Decreto 1006/1985, introducido por la Ley Orgánica 2/2024, de 1 de agosto, que regula la relación laboral especial de los deportistas profesionales. "Estaba tranquila, quería hablar con mi club, de manera pública y privada, todo el mundo sabía que yo quería continuar. Ellos no eran conscientes, o no lo han sido, de que había esta ley. Yo daba por hecho tranquilamente que iba a llegar a Los Ángeles 2028 jugando para el Sabadell", señaló. Su objetivo era regresar a la élite y mantener vivo el sueño de disputar los Juegos Olímpicos de Los Ángeles 2028 con su hija viéndola "en las gradas". Sin embargo, ese camino comenzó a torcerse cuando, en distintas conversaciones, el club vallesano le trasladó que no contaba con ella. "Se referían a una Maica que no es la de hace diez años. He sido madre, me ha cambiado la vida, pero siento que soy una jugadora que puede volver a la élite y seguir soñando con llegar a los Juegos", apuntó. La situación le provocó "muchísimo dolor" y "un cuadro fuerte de ansiedad", según reconoció entre lágrimas. Pese a ello, García insistió en que no guarda "rencor" al club en el que creció y con el que conquistó más de 70 títulos, entre ellos siete Ligas de Campeones, aunque considera que las formas "no han sido las adecuadas". "Mi contrato acababa el 31 de agosto y durante ese tiempo no tuve más comunicación por parte del club. La semana pasada me llamó Recursos Humanos y después me encontré el mensaje de la Seguridad Social de que me habían dado de baja", relató. Según García, las razones que le trasladó el Sabadell fueron "el proyecto deportivo y las decisiones técnicas", argumentos que la jugadora ha contrapuesto a sus más de tres décadas de trayectoria en la entidad. "He liderado muchos proyectos deportivos de este club", recordó. García llegó al Sabadell en 1994, con apenas cuatro años, y ha decidido recurrir a los tribunales para defender su posición. "Me planteo denunciar, llevar a los tribunales al Sabadell. Estoy con mi equipo jurídico y en breve habrá noticias", afirmó. Más allá de su caso particular, la campeona reivindicó la necesidad de facilitar la maternidad en el deporte de élite y defendió que su regreso puede servir de referencia para otras deportistas. "Estoy liderando un cambio social. Antes no tenía un referente, un ejemplo que hubiese sido madre y hubiese vuelto a la élite. Quiero luchar por las próximas niñas o mujeres que quieran ser madres para que tengan el camino más fácil", explicó. La salida del Sabadell no ha supuesto, en cualquier caso, el final de su carrera. Tras conocer la decisión del club, García encontró continuidad en el CN Sant Andreu, con el que ha firmado hasta el verano de 2028. "Tuve propuestas interesantes, pero el Sant Andreu ha sido muy comprensivo con la situación y me ha dado tranquilidad", señaló. La boya reconoció que su última temporada estuvo marcada por un posparto "complicado", por lo que su primer objetivo pasa por recuperar su mejor versión, regresar al máximo nivel y volver a abrir la puerta de la selección española. "Estoy recuperándome para volver al máximo nivel. Es un objetivo personal, conseguir una versión mía mucho mejor y luchar por volver a entrar en las listas cuanto antes", concluyó.

articles.title: Former Hockey Players at University of Michigan Sue, Say They Were Sexually Abused Decades Ago
articles.summary: DETROIT (AP) — More than a dozen former hockey players are suing the University of Michigan, alleging their coach and other staff were aware of sexual hazing that included the forced shaving of their genitals and other abuse by teammates decades ago.
articles.body:
DETROIT (AP) — More than a dozen former hockey players are suing the University of Michigan, alleging their coach and other staff were aware of sexual hazing that included the forced shaving of their genitals and other abuse by teammates decades ago.

"The abuse was ritualized, meticulously planned, and sadistic. ... Enduring sexual abuse was required to be a member of the Michigan Men's Ice Hockey team," attorney Michael Pitt said in a sex discrimination lawsuit filed Wednesday in federal court in Detroit.

The plaintiffs are 16 men who played at Michigan between 1984 and 2001. The lawsuit apparently grew out of conversations among several former teammates in 2024.

The university said the allegations are "disturbing," but denies responsibility.

"To the extent any former student athlete engaged in hazing or other misconduct, they were violating university policy," spokesperson Paul Corliss said in a written statement.

"The university first adopted an official anti-hazing policy in 1982. It was one of the first universities in the country to do so, and it has earned its standing as a leader in this area," he said.

The lawsuit says Red Berenson, who was coach from 1984 to 2017, was aware of the abuse and did not intervene.

Berenson announced the end of "freshman hazing" in 2012, referring to first-year players being forced to carry equipment and eat team meals. He made no mention of physical abuse but acknowledged "captains that got too carried away," according to news reports at the time.

Berenson, 86, declined to comment on the lawsuit Thursday.

"Give me a chance to absorb what's going on," the former NHL player said.

The university in recent years has faced other allegations of sexual misconduct. In 2022, it agreed to pay $490 million to settle claims by more than 1,000 people who said a sports doctor sexually assaulted them during his nearly 40-year career at the school.

articles.title: 2030 Winter Olympics boss Edgar Grospiron departs amid turmoil
articles.summary: Edgar Grospiron leaves his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.
articles.body:
Edgar Grospiron has left his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.

The departure of Grospiron, the 1992 Olympic moguls champion, was confirmed at a meeting of the committee's executive board on Thursday, marking the latest setback in the event's troubled governance.

In a statement, the organising committee said: "His decision to leave the presidency is part of a deliberate, organised and fully assumed transition, taken in the interests of the project and its governance.

"It reflects a shared desire with stakeholders to enable the organisation to quickly enter this new operational phase."

Confirming his departure via a post on LinkedIn, Grospiron said his decision followed "months of tension".

"I draw the conclusion that the conditions are not met for me to continue this," he wrote.

Grospiron's tenure, which began in February 2025, has been plagued by internal turmoil and logistical challenges.

In February 2026, chief executive officer Cyril Linette left the committee, citing "insurmountable disagreements" with Grospiron.

Linette's departure followed a number of other high-profile resignations, including chief operating officer Anne Murac and communications director Arthur Richer.

Budget cuts have plagued the planning process, with Grospiron admitting in February they had "little time, little money".

However, he remained confident he could "deliver a Games that will honour our vision and ambition" provided there was "serenity" and "continuity" from the organising committee.

In May, the committee was forced to shelve the Games' 'ice sports hub' in Nice after the city's mayor, Eric Ciotti, refused to allow OGC Nice's Allianz Riviera Stadium to be converted into a temporary ice rink.

The ice events will now be hosted in Lyon, with the exception of speed skating, which will take place in Heerenveen in the Netherlands.

Two months later, following a tense board meeting in July, French Olympic Committee president Amelie Oudea-Castera told La Tribune Dimanche , external that they were "once again facing governance problems".

Despite another departure from the organising committee, French sports minister Marina Ferrari says there is "no concern about what comes next".

"The bid is continuing to move forward," she told reporters. "Our teams are mobilised and working. We are confident about the future of the Alpes project."

The International Olympic Committee praised Grospiron's "crucial work in laying the foundations for the success" of the Games.

"The IOC will continue working in close collaboration with the organising committee to build on the solid foundations that Mr Grospiron has laid," the statement added.

articles.title: 23 years after Rakesh Yadav, Tanya Chaudhary keeps Baghpat's hammer-throw legacy alive with national record
articles.summary: More sports News: NEW DELHI: It took a minute for Tanya Chaudhary to put her feelings into words. She had very good reason to be overawed by the occasion. With a throw .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: It took a minute for Tanya Chaudhary to put her feelings into words. She had very good reason to be overawed by the occasion. With a throw of 68.35m, the 22-year-old had just broken the national record in hammer throw at the Indian Athletics Series Final.Uttar Pradesh's Chaudhary had multiple aspects to celebrate at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium. She bettered Anushka Yadav's national record of 67.02m set in June. She had edged Anushka (66.34m) in the competition. The record comes within days of her flight to Japan for the Asian Games, which begin on August 19. Lastly, she had just put Baghpat back on the hammer throw map - something Rakesh Yadav had done with a 70.13m throw back in 2003.The 68.35m throw of the chain and iron was a big improvement on her personal best of 63.91m from last year. It was even higher than the 65.60m she had managed at the Inter-University Athletics Championships in January.Coached by Sachin Yadav, her foundations were set at the Shri Krishna Inter College in Baleni, Baghpat. And here, almost 70kms away, her goal of the past three years had been realised."I had been chasing this goal for the past three years. Earlier I had recorded 65m and I had registered it unofficially twice or thrice. But now that I've finally achieved that, and more, I am very pleased," she said with a smile.Her path to the Asian Games was not straightforward.Since January, she has struggled with injuries: a knee issue, a stress injury on the femur bone and an ACL. Then in June, under Bhubaneshwar's floodlights at the Inter-State Championships, she missed the qualification mark by mere two centimetres. Anushka, her UP compatriot, had topped the standings then while also registering the national record."I missed the national record the last time but it's a good thing that we (she and Anushka) come from the same training facility. So, it is a good thing for us to learn and compete with each," she told reporters after pocketing Rs 1 lakh as the winner of the event."That second place finish actually gave me a target, that it has even gotten bigger. That I need to put more effort, work on my shortcomings even more. It's a good thing that we have each other to compete with and improve upon," she continued.Despite the disappointment of missing the qualification mark straightaway, she still found her way into the 503-member Indian contingent for Aichi-Nagoya. The challenge there would be spearheaded by China's Jiale Zhang, who had set the continental record of 78.64m at the Chinese Championships."The target is to obviously do better. Now that I've improved on my personal best, the bare minimum would be to match it. The 70m goal is not far away now. It is now almost 1.5m away."My target this year was to achieve 70m but with injuries I was hampered and affected. But now that I've gained momentum, I am hopeful that I will be able to reach 70m also," she finished.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Jones hoping to prove age is just a number
articles.summary: Double Olympic taekwondo champion Jade Jones, 33, is out to show age is just a number in her next boxing bout against MMA fighter Sheena Bathory.
articles.body:
Double Olympic Taekwondo champion Jade Jones is determined to prove that age will not hold her back as the 33-year-old prepares to box Hungarian MMA fighter Sheena Bathory on 12 September.

Welsh competitor Jones announced herself to the boxing world back in February with a second-round knockout against reality TV star Egypt Criss, before then dispatching Argentine influencer FederiKita in May to take her record to 2-0.

After her winning start, Jones, will now face her toughest test yet as she prepares to face Bathory for the Misfits super middleweight title at Newcastle's Utilita Arena.

Since beginning her boxing career at 31-years-old, the fearless Jones hopes she can inspire others with her journey.

"I wanted to show people that you shouldn't be scared of failing and trying. People do think 'oh you're 33', and I did start to feel like that at the end of my Taekwondo career, that I'm older now and I've kind of passed the line," said Jones.

"But with this growth journey I've been on, I've realised you are only as old as you feel and how old you tell yourself. I don't know how good I'm going to be, I could've got knocked out in the first fight, but I'm doing this."

Jones, from Bodelwyddan in north Wales, added: "I've only just started and I'm not scared to fail and hopefully it will show more people that you can start again, you can try something different.

"Your life isn't over when you get to a certain age. It can start whenever you want it to start."

Jones captured the hearts of audiences during the 2012 London Olympics, when she became the first Briton to win a gold medal in taekwondo.

She defended her title four years later at the Rio 2016 Games, becoming back-to-back champion in the 57kg weight class and etching her name into history.

Despite a stellar career in the sport, Jones discussed the difficulty of walking away and her struggles post retirement.

"People don't realise that when you're in a sport you reach the highest of the highs, for the Olympic gold, every part of my day was about winning that. How you sleep, how you eat, your mind is consumed with it," Jones said.

"Then you reach the pinnacle of the sport, you're at the top of the mountain, you've won the Olympics, you're the best of the best and then to go back to normal mundane life, it's tough, it's like there is something missing.

"I've always had that purpose, that drive, that direction and knowing exactly what I want and what I'm going for. All your day revolves around it, so when it's missing it's hard for athletes. Just two months after retirement I felt lost, it was tough."

Despite becoming a two-time Olympic champion, she could not make it a third, suffering early round exits at the Tokyo and Paris Olympics and drawing her remarkable taekwondo career to a close.

But it was not long until Jones would take the plunge into the boxing world, one she is determined to shake up.

"Loads of people told me to retire and just go off into the sunset and enjoy your life kind of thing. But I still had that itch, still had that drive. I'm 33, but I feel like a young 33 and I felt like I just had a lot more to do," said Jones.

Jones was also recently diagnosed with ADHD , and insists that it has played a part in her becoming hooked with the sport.

"It kind of came out of nowhere, I thought I might try boxing, it maybe sort of started as a joke but I thought I'll try it. Well I recently found out I've got ADHD so that explains a lot," she added.

"As soon as I started, I was hooked on the improvement, hooked on the whole thing of entering the ring and the fear of it's just you and that person and someone could get knocked out and the thrill of it.

"I absolutely love to fight, love to train and love to try and become the best at something."

Despite comprehensive victories in her first two professional bouts, her next opponent, Bathory, will pose much more of a threat than her previous challengers.

The Hungarian secured a first round knockout on her debut fight and has also competed in the controversial TV show and competition, Power Slap - which is part-owned by UFC chief executive Dana White.

Jones' first two opponents were social media influencers taking to the ring, and despite the challenge Bathory poses, she is relishing the opportunity to enter the arena once more.

"She's a really tough opponent and she's got a martial arts background. But I'm just super excited to get back out there," the Welsh fighter said.

"I feel like this will show another level to my boxing skills. It will give me a tougher fight and another opportunity for me to keep showing what I'm about."

Jones has been training under the guidance of Stephen 'Swifty' Smith and his brothers at Liverpool's 4 Corners Gym and is confident her experience will pay dividends.

"I've done it, I've been in that ring, I've got experience in that environment with that pressure, so it's about handling the nerves and doing what I've been doing in the gym with the Smith brothers," she added.

Beginning with her bout against Bathory, Jones must navigate the challenge of facing tougher opponents.

With that comes an added sense of danger, but Jones has brushed this off and praised the people around her for their support.

"It's a very dangerous sport, the more stories you hear of bad things happening, people going into comas it is very scary, it makes you realise it's a brutal sport. You don't play boxing as they say," Jones said.

"But it's you against them, everyone knows what they're getting into, you've just got to train your best and always protect yourself.

"My view is you can get knocked over crossing the street. Everyone has their own choice in life. If you've got the right trainer and the right people, you always try and stay safe."

Jones and Bathory will face each other on the undercard of Jordan McCann v Big Stacks on 12 September at Utilita Arena, Newcastle.
